title: Spay & Neuter Recovery: Timeline & Aftercare Tips
summary: Learn the spay and neuter recovery timeline for dogs and cats, what a healing incision looks like, warning signs to watch for, and how to help them heal.

[Spaying or neutering](https://petcube.com/blog/pet-neutering-and-spaying/) your pet involves anesthesia, and the recovery period can seem scary for you as a pet parent. Knowing what your fur child can and can’t do after surgery will make their recovery easier and more manageable for you.


Dr. Griffin says:


> “Spay-neuter programs represent a crucial component of community efforts to reduce the sheltering and euthanasia of unwanted and unowned cats and dogs.”


**Content:**


1. Spay & Neuter Recovery Timeline: How Long It Takes and How to Care for Your Dog or Cat
2. What a Healing Spay Incision Should Look Like (Day by Day)
3. Warning Signs: Infection, Seroma, Hernia, Lumps & When to Call the Vet
4. Behavior, Appetite & Comfort After Surgery: What's Normal and How to Help
5. Conclusion


## Spay & Neuter Recovery Timeline: How Long It Takes and How to Care for Your Dog or Cat


You may find that your pet is[sore](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-in-pain/) after the operation. Most veterinary clinics give pain medication during the procedure, which should last 24 hours and keep them comfortable. Pain medication is usually sent home with your pet for the next 3 days to help manage pain and inflammation.


It is important to encourage your cat or dog to[eat](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-not-eating/) and drink, starting with only small amounts of food and water at a time.


Keeping your pet quiet for a few days after the procedure, in an area with a comfortable temperature, may be a challenge if you have an active dog or cat, but it will help them recover more smoothly. Many animals struggle to regulate their own[body temperature](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-normal-body-temperature/) after anesthesia, so it’s up to you as their pet parent to keep them at a comfortable temperature.


Check the wound daily for any discharge, bleeding, or swelling. Some dogs and cats dislike the feel of the sutures and try to remove their own stitches. If you notice[excessive licking](https://petcube.com/blog/why-do-dogs-lick-everything/) , a cone of shame is recommended to stop them from pulling their stitches out and causing damage.


[Research](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S109002332500200X?ref=petcube.com) shows that:


> “Surgical site infections (SSIs) remain a common complication that increases morbidity and mortality.”


- **Days 1–3:** This is the riskiest time for the incision to open. It is very important to limit activity and keep your pet as calm as possible.
- **Days 4–7:** Any bruising or inflammation should start to fade, and the swelling should go down. By day 7, many pets feel much better, but it’s still important to restrict activity and jumping onto furniture.
- **Days 8–14:** The skin has closed completely, and any external sutures are generally removed at 10–14 days. The incision line should appear flat and dry. A small, firm bump under the skin is normal where the suture material was placed internally and the surrounding tissue has knitted back together.
- **By week 6:** Full internal healing should have taken place, and your pet can return to all normal activity.


## What a Healing Spay Incision Should Look Like (Day by Day)


For female cats and dogs, a healing spay incision should look like this:


- Skin edges that touch and look clean and slightly pink. Mild bruising can be present.
- As the days go on, a small raised area under the skin can be a sign of a seroma or a reaction to the suture material used to close the muscle and skin layers. If it stays small and doesn’t grow from day to day, there’s no cause for concern.
- It is important to keep the incision site clean and dry, which means no bathing or swimming until the sutures are removed 10–14 days after the procedure.
- A small amount of dried blood or a thin scab is normal.


Taking a photo of the incision every day can help you spot any subtle changes that may be taking place.


Dr. Cavanaugh says:


> “Wound healing complications are ubiquitous in veterinary clinical practice regardless of the skill level of the attending practitioner. Timely and accurate identification and mitigation of contributing causes are of paramount importance to the successful surgical management of the wounded companion animal.”


## Warning Signs: Infection, Seroma, Hernia, Lumps & When to Call the Vet


A healthy, healing spay or castration wound stays closed with minimal swelling and bruising. Note that when a male cat is neutered, no skin sutures are placed, since the incision is very small and heals well without them.


Warning signs to look out for:


- Redness that is spreading rather than staying localized to the incision site
- The area around the incision is hot to the touch, which can indicate an infection
- The incision opening, or large gaps between skin sutures
- Excessive swelling (seroma)
- Something protruding from the incision site (a hernia or lump)
- Pus, discharge, or bleeding from the incision
- A bad smell from the incision site
- Excessive licking, which will cause more swelling and redness


If you notice any of the above, make a follow-up appointment with the veterinarian who performed the surgery. Castrations in mature male dogs tend to bruise and swell more than in younger dogs. Placing an ice pack wrapped in a cloth on the scrotum for short periods can help, and a cone of shame will be needed to stop him from licking excessively.


## Behavior, Appetite & Comfort After Surgery: What's Normal and How to Help


Dogs and cats are placed under general anesthesia for sterilization procedures. Their body needs time to clear the anesthetic from their system, and this can take a few days. Your pet may be[groggy](https://petcube.com/blog/lethargy-in-dogs/) and[sleepier than usual](https://petcube.com/blog/why-dogs-sleep-all-day/) for the first few days after surgery. Because the reproductive organs have been removed, there will be less estrogen and testosterone in their system. Remember that removing the reproductive organs does not remove your pet’s[personality](https://petcube.com/blog/neutering-and-spaying-calm-a-dog/) .


After sterilization, your pet will be more likely to[gain weight](https://petcube.com/blog/obesity-in-dogs/) . It is important to feed only according to the recommended feeding guidelines for your pet’s food and to avoid table scraps. Instead, use appropriate[low-fat treats](https://petcube.com/blog/healthy-treats/) . A follow-up weigh-in at your vet 3–6 months after surgery is a good way to monitor for weight gain.


The[Petcube App](https://petcube.com/promo/atp-w2w/?ref=petcube.com) is the only app you need to assist with at-home care. You can track changes to your pet’s surgical site, as well as their health and habits. You will also have access to certified vets for any guidance you may need on changes in behavior or symptoms.


## Conclusion


Sterilizing your pet at the correct age has many long-term health benefits and is well worth the recovery period and extra attention your pet will need during that time.


In her[article](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.2147/VMRR.S53264?ref=petcube.com) on sterilization, Dr. Howe says:


> “In veterinary practice, surgical sterilization of cats and dogs is one of the most common surgical procedures performed. Routine spaying/castrating is often performed because of its value in preventing reproductive tract disease, including pyometra and mammary neoplasia in female cats and dogs, and benign prostatic hyperplasia and testicular neoplasia in male dogs.”
